pr_body:
HotThreads has wait and blocked time accounting functionality, however the reported timings for the "wait" and "block" reports are always 0, because thread contention monitoring isn't enabled in the JVM. This change fixes that by enabling/disabling thread contention monitoring, while we are running the timing capture logic. 

Apart from fixing the wait/block time accounting bug, this PR also restricts the reported thread timings to values >= 0 to fix the test failures reported in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/72376, which relate to CPU thread migration.

I did a small refactor to eliminate the code duplication in the timing capture logic, remove unused variables and add more unit tests for the refactored logic.

Closes #72376

I looked this particular failure and I believe the error can happen in the event where a thread execution migrates a CPU while running the test. This would be a rare event on the platform where this test was run (CPU affinity is typically respected by the OS scheduler), however it's definitely something that would happen.

The IllegalArgumentException that's thrown comes from constructing a TimeValue with a duration less than -1, in this case -5160. The only place in `HotThreads.java` where we create a TimeValue object with a variable duration, is while constructing the output for CPU % per thread, i.e:

```
            sb.append(String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%n%4.1f%% (%s out of %s) %s usage by thread '%s'%n",
                percent, TimeValue.timeValueNanos(time), interval, type, threadName));
```

The `time` variable is calculated by taking a delta from the two CPU times, before and after the HotThreads sampling thread slept for 500ms. The way the JVM implements the API `ThreadMXBean.getThreadCpuTime` on Linux is by using `clock_gettime` with the `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID` parameter. This Linux API is implemented on x86-64 (or x86 in general) is via reading the internal CPU TSC registers. If a thread migrates a CPU during the 500ms sampler thread sleep, the calculated delta would be always bogus, and in case where most of the thread execution happened on the earlier CPU, the delta value calculated would be negative.

This issue with `clock_gettime` is documented here: https://linux.die.net/man/3/clock_gettime. Specifically the `NOTE for SMP systems` section.

The test failure because of this implementation limitation will be resolved when PR https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/77392 is merged. It's not possible to calculate an accurate thread CPU time when a thread migrates a CPU, or in the event when a thread ID is reused on thread death (e.g. typical on Windows). Therefore, the PR mention above always caps the minimum delta to 0, effectively discarding the HotThreads result for this thread in the rare event of thread CPU migration or thread ID reuse.
